Question: What are the legal consequences of impersonating the police?
Answer: RCW 9A.60.040 Criminal impersonation in the first degree. (1) A person is guilty of criminal impersonation in the first degree if the person: (a) Assumes a false identity and does an act in his or her assumed character with intent to defraud another or for any other unlawful purpose; or (b) Pretends to be a representative of some person or organization or a public servant and does an act in his or her pretended capacity with intent to defraud another or for any other unlawful purpose. (2) Criminal impersonation in the first degree is a class C felony. Criminal impersonation in the second degree. (1) A person is guilty of criminal impersonation in the second degree if the person: (a)(i) Claims to be a law enforcement officer or creates an impression that he or she is a law enforcement officer; and (ii) Under circumstances not amounting to criminal impersonation in the first degree, does an act with intent to convey the impression that he or she is acting in an official capacity and a reasonable person would believe the person is a law enforcement officer; or (b) Falsely assumes the identity of a veteran or active duty member of the armed forces of the United States with intent to defraud for the purpose of personal gain or to facilitate any unlawful activity. (2) Criminal impersonation in the second degree is a gross misdemeanor.

Question: How is it legal for the cops to use a criminal as a confidential informant? How is this not considered bribery and/or entrapment?
Answer: Most confidential informants (CIs) are criminals. They get caught with the goods and are persuaded to give up information in exchange for a plea bargain or lighter sentence. It is completely lawful to use a CI in this manner. Bribery is the offer or acceptance of consideration (usually money, but could be sex or any other commodity) in exchange for doing something the government employee is not supposed to do, or failing to do something they are supposed to do. The classic situation is the cop who is paid to look the other way while criminal activity he is supposedly to detect and interdict takes place. Entrapment is a practice in which a law enforcement agent or an agent of the state induces a person to commit a crime that the person would have otherwise been unlikely or unwilling to commit.[1] It "is the conception and planning of an offense by an officer or agent, and the procurement of its commission by one who would not have perpetrated it except for the trickery, persuasion or fraud of the officer or state agent".[2] (the above from Wikipedia) If a cop sends a CI to your house to buy drugs from you and you sell them the drugs, it’s probably not entrapment unless you are brand new at the illicit drug trade and just had that meth lying around. If you were predisposed to involvement in the illicit drug trade (e.g. you just promoted from user to dealer), you’re toast. The use of CIs to make controlled drug buys is a long-accepted practice in narcotics investigations. It not only yields arrests, but it makes it more hazardous for the drug user. Is my dealer a CI? Is my customer? You won’t know until someone shows you a badge. You can avoid the dangers of interacting with CIs by obeying the law. For example, I’m not worried about a CI trying to get me to sell him meth or buying meth from a CI because I don’t use or sell meth. This approach has worked out very well for me in terms of not violating the law.

Question: Have you ever been given morphine at a hospital or as a prescription and how would you describe in detail what it was like?
Answer: I was given morphine after surgery. The surgery was one that had a historically difficult and painful recovery. The medication was dispensed through a patient-controlled anesthesia (PCA) device, where I could get a fresh dose by pushing a button. After getting maxed out for the hour, the device locked me out until I was “eligible” for another dose. I have never been a fan of chemical recreation. I’ve never used marijuana or any recreational drug. I voluntarily gave up alcohol in college because I didn’t like the feeling of being drunk or having the hangover afterward. I rarely take pain medication, to include OTC drugs like aspirin and ibuprofen. My first impression of morphine was “I can see how people can get hooked on this.” I felt floaty, wonderful. I still felt pain, but I didn’t care. I really liked where I was and wished I could stay there. This brief experience was considerable insight into the psychology of addiction. I wasn’t given any anti-emetic in my IV, which I later learned was a standard practice. This is because morphine often causes vomiting. When I ate my dinner, some of it came right back up. Vomiting is, for me at least, usually a traumatic experience, accompanied by nausea and discomfort. This vomiting was almost passive, no more uncomfortable than burping. I was very disappointed when the nurse came in and told me they would have to switch me to Demerol since the morphine was causing vomiting. The Demerol yielded no euphoria, but it also didn’t touch my pain. My surgery was on a Friday morning, and I wouldn’t see my surgeon until Monday. As soon as he showed up, they discharged me with oral Vicodin for pain control. It didn’t work any better than the Demerol. I haven’t had any morphine since that episode 30 years ago, mainly because I haven’t had any injuries or surgeries to need it. But, if I wind up with a painful injury again, I’ll be asking for morphine.

Question: From a lawyer's perspective, citizens should never talk to police officers. From a police perspective, they want compliant citizens. Where is the middle ground? How much should a citizen speak to a police officer, even if they often are being tricky?
Answer: I have no fear of speaking to police officers because I have committed no crimes. The last time I spoke to a police officer in any sort of adversarial setting was when I was pulled over by a highway patrol trooper. I had a late-night craving for tacos and took my dog with me on a run to Taco Bell. It was a warm summer night, and I had all the windows down for the dog and the radio up loud. When I saw the reds and blues come on, I assessed the situation and thought, “I would have pulled me over, too.” He said I was driving 42 MPH in a 35 zone, which surprised me not at all. Actually, I thought the speed limit was higher. The trooper asked me for my paperwork and made small talk for a minute. He was assessing me as a drunk driver. I’ve made hundreds of DUI arrests and knew exactly what he was doing. I had no hesitation about answering any of his questions as I had nothing stronger to drink than Coca-Cola. I don’t drink alcohol. Within a minute or two, I was back on my way home. If I had a suspended driver’s license, no insurance, had been drinking or smoking weed, or had a dead body stashed in the trunk, I might have been less forthcoming. However, I know that most crooks lie badly. They tell inconsistent stories that get blown up as soon as the officer runs their driver’s license or criminal history. I think most cops appreciate civility. They don’t expect you to confess to all your crimes. Just don’t tell outrageous lies, don’t threaten the cop with your lawyer or your friend the mayor, and don’t try to conceal your open beer or joint in the car seat, because the cop is going to see it and you’re going to have a damaged car seat. Roll down the window (don’t do the “I can talk to you through the upper two inches gap” game), hand the cop your license, registration and insurance when asked for it, and if you don’t want to answer other questions, just say so. This is a business transaction, nothing more. No matter what happens, the words “polite and cooperative” in an arrest report or in the officer’s notes on a citation have never hurt anyone in court.

Question: How are courts/law enforcement dealing with the modern American phenomenon of "I'm mentally ill" being used as a universal excuse for abusive criminal behavior?
Answer: The classic insanity defense shows up a lot on TV dramas, but it’s not used that often in the real world. “Sane” is a legal term, not a medical one. A sane person knows what they are doing, and knows whether it is right or wrong. To be ruled “insane,” a mental health professional (usually a psychologist or psychiatrist) must perform an examination and make a determination as to whether the person can understand those principles. Defendants can try to argue they are of diminished capacity because of their depression, their anxiety, or their illicit drug use or alcoholism, but those defenses rarely work. You’re supposed to seek help for your depression or anxiety before you embark on a life of crime. Voluntary intoxication by drugs or alcohol has never been a valid defense.

Question: When the police are looking for a missing person, what things (categories) make that missing person classed as "vulnerable"?

Children, who are usually of inferior size and intellect, almost always qualify. Senior citizens might be classed as vulnerable if they are physically handicapped or suffer from cognitive decline. Other mentally or physically handicapped people could be classified as vulnerable, as could people suffering an intense personal trauma, such as the recent death of a loved one.

Question: Are detectives a lot smarter than patrol officers?

With the exception of federal agent types who work for agencies where there are no uniformed personnel, all detectives were uniformed patrolmen first. In many cases, they’ll be uniformed patrolmen again. Smaller agencies often rotate the detective assignment, so whoever is the detective has that assignment for a year or three, then moves back to patrol to be replaced by another patrolman. Detectives may be assigned to the role for showing exception skill in investigations. They may also be there because they keep falling asleep if they’re assigned to nighttime patrol. They could have child care issues that are incompatible with a rotating day/night patrol schedule. They might have good political connections to get them assigned to a more prestigious role, one that doesn’t require “chasing the radio” by going call to call. The detective’s job may appear more cerebral than the patrol officer’s, but most arrests will be made by patrol officers, even those on warrants applied for by the detectives. If the detective obtains an arrest warrant but does not know immediately where to locate the suspect, they’ll route it to be filed in Records, and their suspect will get busted the next time patrol runs across him. I worked for a police department with 300 sworn officers. Three of us were card-carrying members of Mensa. None of us were detectives, mostly by choice.

Question: If there has just been a robbery (example) and there is a description of the vehicle, appearance and/or clothing of a person and officers encounter someone with that description. Can this person be arrested?

If the situation was such that the officer could say why he felt the suspect could be armed, he could pat down the suspect for weapons. This is a “Terry Stop,” named for the decision in Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968). A Terry stop does not permit the officer to remove the suspect from the location he was stopped without the suspect’s consent. To get probable cause for arrest, the officer would do a field interview of the suspect, including taking a photo. The photo would then be included in a “six pack” of photos to show the victim to see if he recognized anyone in the array. If so, the police could obtain an arrest warrant for the suspect. In the alternative, the officer could have another officer pick up the victim and drive by the location where the suspect was stopped to make an identification or say, “No, that’s not the guy.” These identifications are more iffy, as the suggestion that the suspect has been stopped by the police and the lack of other possible suspects is more suggestive of guilt.

Question: Can the police arrest you on a false allegation if there is no proof?
Answer: First, you have to get the order of what everyone knew and when they knew it. Let’s say that you and I have some sort of feud ongoing. I bang my head into something at work and have a noticeable wound. I go to the police and make a report that the wound came from you attacking me with a heavy bookend. The police take the report and submit it to the prosecutor’s office, which issues a warrant for your arrest. You get arrested and demand a trial. The police acted in good faith, accepting the plausible explanation for the wound from me, the apparent victim/complainant. I signed the report form, attesting that my statements were true, and understanding that filing a false police report is a crime in itself. At trial, you get to challenge my story. I’m not compelled to testify, but if I don’t, there is no case, and you can rightfully ask for a dismissal of the charges. If I do testify, you can cross-examine me and try to find holes in my story. You can then testify in your behalf. Maybe you have an alibi, proving you were someplace else when I said you hit me. Maybe you have a witness to support your story. You can subpoena them to testify, and they can’t refuse unless their testimony would incriminate them (for example, if the two of you were smoking weed in a state that still criminalized it, the witness could refuse to say what the two of you were doing). Maybe you can show from the interactions that you could not have hit me in such a way as to cause that wound. Maybe you can find a workman's compensation report showing I was injured at work, and not by you. Of course, if you can’t put on any of this evidence, or if your presentation is lame, you might be found guilty of something you didn’t do. So, if the police are presented with a reasonable story about a crime, and the reporting person is willing to sign the statement or crime report, yes, you can be arrested on a false allegation. “Proof” comes at trial, not at the crime scene or the police station front desk.

Question: What would be worse for the cardiovascular system, smoking an entire pack of cigarettes, drinking a whole bottle of wine, or a six pack of beer?
Answer: The cigarettes, I think. One cigarette has enough nicotine to kill you if it is ingested all at once. You can’t smoke one that fast, so the administration of the drug is more gradual. Repeated does of nicotine over and over can overstimulate the heart. The wine and beer are of relatively low alcohol content. People often ingest that much wine and beer at one sitting.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: I have a drug test today and the only thing I smoke is weed and I need to get it out of my system today. I have a test at 2 pm. Does anyone have anything that will help?
Answer: At this point, prayer is about your only option. Rumor has it that God is not especially charitable to potheads. Consider which is more important to you: pot, or passing the drug test. You can only have one. If weed is more important, you’re likely addicted.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: Do the police have the right to pull you over more than once for no insurance (4 times in 4 weeks)?
Answer: Every time you drive without insurance, you commit a new offense. Think about it—you could get into an accident on every trip, and every one of those accidents would be uninsured. You don’t get any grace period because you got a “no insurance” ticket earlier today, or yesterday, or last week. The state expects you to get your car insured, or stop driving it until you do. Meanwhile, every one of those “no insurance” tickets can result in a fine, a license suspension, and/or a registration suspension. Eventually, one of the cops who stops you is going to impound your car to keep you from driving until the car is insured.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: What is the easiest gun to use for protection? I have arthritis in my hands.
Answer: A medium-frame revolver, such as a S&W Model 60, is a better choice than a semi-automatic. It is more forgiving of poor grip strength or hand position.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: If the Scottsdale police say most of their 110 million dollar annual budget goes towards salaries but they only have 400 total employees with an average salary of 75k then what is covered up and why isn't anyone being held accountable?
Answer: Personnel costs are nearly always the lion’s share of any business budget, and always the most costly item in a people-intensive industry like policing. $30M (400 x $75K) for salaries sounds low to me. Typically, salaries are between 50%-80% of a law enforcement agency’s operating budget. But, let’s see where some of that extra money might have gone. Salary is only one component of compensation. The agency is usually required to make a contribution to the employee’s retirement fund—maybe 8%-10% of salary. There’s another $3M. Health and dental benefits could run as high as $1500 per month per employee. That’s another $7.2M per year. A typical uniform allowance is $1000 per year. Say that 70% of SPD employees wear uniforms. That another $280,000. I’d estimate that a 400-man agency needs at least 175 cars. A fully-equipped police car costs at least $60,000, with a service life of about four years. That’s $2.625M for new cars every year, assuming none of them get wrecked. Add 10% for wrecked or otherwise disabled cars, so $2,887,500 per year. Those cars drive 25,000–50,000 miles per year. They get about 11 miles per gallon. Say gas costs $4.00 per gallon. That’s $137,000. I’d estimate it costs at least $500,000 per year to maintain a shop to service and repair vehicles. Does SPD own its building? If not, what are they paying each month to retire the bond that was used to purchase it? How much does it cost to heat and cool the building? How often does it need repair? Do the A/C units, furnace, roof, plumbing need repair or replacement? Officers have to be sent to training now and then. Forms have to be printed. Photocopiers and printers have to be purchased and serviced. There are the costs of running any other business. Are you seeing where that money might be spent?

Name: Tim Dees
Question: How many times do I have to contact the FBI and state police before they do anything?
Answer: Much depends on what you’re trying to report. Law enforcement agencies regularly receive reports of incidents that are not crimes, and therefore do not fall within their mission. There are also many reports that are simply nonsensical and not worthy of investigation. Reports based on the mere suspicion of a citizen are generally insufficient to open a case. Consider whether a reasonable person would view your report as credible. That might make your situation more understandable.

Question: I live in California. I'm 17 years old. Can I volunteer to shadow a medical professional in the hospital? If so, can I choose what type of medical professional to shadow?
Answer: Many hospitals and clinics will refuse such a “volunteer” applicant because of patient privacy laws. Access to medical procedures and records is limited to those with a need to know. That doesn’t include a “like to watch.” A 17-year-old volunteering in a hospital is going to be pushing wheelchairs and signing people into clinics. You may see a procedure occasionally. I was a teenage hospital volunteer at a place where the ER was staffed by moonlighting Army doctors who were used to being assisted by medics only a few years older than me. One let me put about six sutures into the head of an unconscious drunk. It was the coolest thing I’d done up to that point in my life. I don’t think you would get that experience now.

Question: Is it considered impersonation a sheriff or police officer if my mother says "this is the police department" towards a known or unknown caller in order to scare off the person to not let them call back?

Question: Is it illegal to post picture of yourself in a police uniform on social media even though you’re not actually a police officer?
Answer: If your dress-up game would suggest to a reasonable person that you are an actual police officer, then you would be committing a crime. Context, appearance, and captioning have considerable influence here.

Question: If a law enforcement agency decides that they won’t offer a wealthy client a police escort could a private security company hire off duty officers to drive a private security vehicle but instead of using ambers the officer could use emergency lights?
Answer: Whether anything like this can happen depends on local law and custom. Police agencies can generally provide escorts at their discretion. The U.S. Navy Blue Angels crew usually gets a police escort from their hotel to the airfield. High-profile rock stars may get an escort if there is a likelihood that fans will try to stop or otherwise interfere with the limo or whatever they’re riding in. Some places allow their officers to work for private security companies or individual businesses, often working in uniform and driving a marked patrol car. Some officers make more money from these “pay jobs” than from their police salary. My former employer allowed private businesses to hire off duty officers to work in uniform and sometimes driving a marked patrol car for events like marathons, parades, and movie locations. The officer got whatever his regular overtime rate was. The city got about 150% of the top overtime rate. Amber lights versus red and blues? Again, it depends on the local jurisdiction.

Question: If someone made a false police report about Jimmy and Jimmy has video proof and witnesses of it being false, Jimmy wants this removed, what should/can he do?

Question: If shared online an essay article I wrote, how do I protect my claim to being the author of it in case someone tries to steal it? Is there a system that can detect plagiarism or theft of this kind? When I was in high school, I heard MyAccess can.

Question: Can I go back & have a case examined where I plead guilty when I was minor but ended up being charged as an adult from being illegally searched as a passenger in a vehicle when I did not give my consent nor was a search warrant provided?
Answer: Probably not. You would have to demonstrate there had been some huge injustice that resulted. Your claim that you were “illegally searched as a passenger in a vehicle when I did not give my consent nor was a search warrant provided” is likely wishful thinking. Most people searched in the field do not give their consent. They are frisked for weapons, and information developed during the investigation amounts to sufficient probable cause to do a more extensive search. It would be very rare to secure a search warrant to search a passenger on a traffic stop. The context of your question also suggests that the search was fruitful, and produced evidence of a crime that led to you being charged. That tends to support the officer’s belief that evidence would be recovered during the search, which is more or less the definition of probable cause. If you’re going to use contraband drugs, do it at home. Don’t carry them on your person, and don’t have them in your car. The home is the most protected premise under the Fourth Amendment,. It’s the hardest premise to secure a search warrant.

Question: The United States Marshals Service is a federal agency that protects the deputy attorney general and federal judges and court justices and has firearms and jurisdiction in the US but can US Marshals be armed with firearms on foreign security details?

Question: I’m 34, Irish, working as an electrician in London, I am looking to move to America to become a police officer but not sure is it possible, or how possible?
Answer: It can be done. I worked with several men who emigrated to the United States to become police officers. We had a couple of Brits, a Pakistani, and an East German. All were fine officers. You first have to secure a visa that allows you to work in the U.S., assuming you aren’t wealthy enough to support yourself without working. You’ll need to work as an electrician or in some other occupation while you apply for U.S. citizenship. Once you become a U.S. citizen, you can apply for police jobs. A few agencies in the U.S. are entertaining applications from people with resident alien status, e.g. non-citizens. I don’t have a list. That is another possibility for you.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: When some US cops wrongfully arrest people over an argument over lack of probable cause, knowing that the person will be cleared, but not without paying bond or suffering days locked up in custody, isn't that precisely what the cop wants in revenge?
Answer: You seem to be describing what we used to call “contempt of cop.” Abuse the officer enough, and he will find some reason to arrest you. Making an arrest without probable cause is a career-ender. It opens the officer and his agency to civil lawsuits and federal civil rights claims, which will often result in the payment of six-figure damages. What separates contempt of cop from false arrest is discretion. Police officers have wide discretion in how to handle most situations in the field. Community policing training emphasizes that making an arrest is only one possible solution, and often is the least desirable option. There are many circumstances where an officer has more than enough probable cause for an arrest, but chooses some other path, to include warning the individual about their behavior and sending them on their way. Cops are human beings, and subject to the same emotional push buttons as everyone else. When the cop encounters someone who is being as obnoxious as possible toward the cop because they think they are immune from any enforcement action, it’s only natural for the cop to consider the option that will show Mr. Personality just how wrong he is about being immune. The cop might have to get creative, which means using the law in unconventional ways. There is nothing illegal about this, especially if Mr. P. has been warned about his behavior and the possible consequences. Example: we had both a state law and a city ordinance titled “Failure to obey a police officer.” Ominous as that might sound, it covered the behavior of people on the roadway. A police officer directing traffic can order motorists and pedestrians to move against posted directional signs of a one-way street, to stop where stopping is usually prohibited, and to do just about anything else to facilitate safety of traffic and people. If you’re a pedestrian on a public sidewalk, you have considerable freedom to walk, stop, or dance as you please, so long as you don’t impede others. Step onto the pavement, and the rules change. If the cop orders you to stop and get back on the sidewalk, that is an entirely lawful order. Refuse it, and you’re subject to citation or arrest. You can probably see where this is going. Say I’m on a traffic stop, and Mr. Personality happens by to engage in the exercise of his First Amendment rights. He shouts to everyone how I am a jackbooted thug (despite hearing that phrase so often, I never knew cops to wear jackboots, or run into many citizens who could describe them), how I am harassing an innocent civilian, and shouting unhelpful and mostly incorrect legal advice to my violator and the occupants of his car. I ask Mr. P. several times to tone it down, and he becomes more defiant. Eventually, he decides to move in a bit, and steps off the curb. I warn him to get back on the sidewalk. He comes back with some variation of “Whatcha gonna do about it, pig?” Bingo. Handcuffs time. Mr. P. gets to cool his heels in my prisoner cage while I finish the traffic stop. He may decide to resist arrest, which I and the other cops present will regard as quality entertainment and will result in additional charges. Then, he becomes a guest of the county detention facility, screaming all the way about his violated rights. He eventually gets to talk to a lawyer (despite their claims, these guys seldom have lawyers on retainer), who tells him he should have stayed on the sidewalk, and in the future, being less vocal during police operations would be advisable. There was lots of probable cause to arrest Mr. Personality. He created the situation himself.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: Don't you think it's time that every time you see a police officer/s, stop and say "Thank You for putting your life on the line every day for us, thank you"?
Answer: I’ve never had anyone say that to me. I did get some “Thank you for your service.” This got to be more popular after 9/11 and the Gulf War. Comments like this are just folks’ way of reaching out to say they acknowledge your work and appreciate the risk you take in doing it. A couple of weeks ago, I had some tree service guys at my house. They spent most of one day trimming back the branches and leaves of three fully mature willow trees, removing over five tons of waste. I made it a point to thank them for doing a difficult and hazardous job that I didn’t know how to do, and probably wouldn’t be very good at if I did. I also supplied an ice chest full of chilled sports drinks and bottled water, which they seemed to appreciate (most of it was gone by the end of the day). I try to acknowledge and give dignity to professional work, even if it’s “blue collar” and without a lot of social status attached. People like to know they’re appreciated. Comments like the one you referenced are just one way of doing that for police officers. If you don’t want to say it to cops, don’t.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: How much over the speed limit do most officers let you go before pulling you over?
Answer: This is a magic question, often asked on Quora in other forms. The motorist knows what the speed limit sign says, but how much can they exceed the speed limit and get away with it? What’s the real speed limit? Of course, once we have established the real speed limit, how fast can I drive before I get stopped? It must be unreasonable to stop me for only one mile an hour over the real speed limit, so what’s the real, real speed limit? There are somewhere between 800,000 and 900,000 law enforcement officers in the United States, although not all of those are assigned to roles that include traffic enforcement. I have never heard an agency or an agency trainer tell an officer that they can start writing tickets at 5,10,15 or whatever number you choose over the speed limit. Everyone establishes their own tolerance level, and that can change with weather, type of vehicle (the Corvette is probably going to get more attention than the VW Bug), other driving behaviors, traffic conditions, and other factors. Just how charitable the officer is feeling that day might have something to do with it, too. The truth: there is no standard. Everybody picks their own. My ticket avoidance strategy lies with setting my cruise control to the posted speed limit (not X miles over) and waving at the state trooper as I go by. Despite the claims of other drivers, I have never had my “doors blown off” by other, faster-moving vehicles. I pass some of them, and some of them pass me. I spend most of my time in the rightmost traffic lanes. I have had two speeding tickets. I got them both during the Nixon Administration, when I did not have a vehicle with cruise control and frankly I was a bit more aggressive at driving than I am now. I paid both tickets, because I was in fact speeding (on one, the CHP officer cut me a substantial break on my observed speed). I get to my destinations a few minutes behind people who have much higher insurance premiums than I have.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: Is it credible that Derek Chauvin was a victim of excessive sentencing and was actually a scapegoat and victim of a show trial?
Answer: Chauvin was more of a victim of an organizational culture that permitted excessive force. There was no special malice apparent between Chauvin and George Floyd. Chauvin had been conditioned to depersonalize heavy drug users and possibly Black people so that he could use unreasonable force against them and have no moral conflict about it. This is not something that takes place overnight. It’s the result of unintended psychological conditioning in dealing with an underclass of people who are regarded as more than expendable. Rather than being expendable, they’re undesirable, trash that needs to be taken to the curb for pickup. I expect that Chauvin had used similar force against similar suspects many times before, but most of his previous victims didn’t die, and the incidents were not so well-documented on video. Most police misconduct can be traced back to poor supervision. Field supervisors—usually sergeants—feel unmotivated to intervene or even be aware of what their subordinates are doing. If you don’t bother to get to calls, observe the actions of your cops, and act when you see something that is contrary to policy, you have a very easy job. Sergeants like having an easy job, and if they don’t report any misconduct, their lieutenants and captains can happily report that all is well in the kingdom. Chauvin might have been the victim of an overreaction by the court in seeing such callous behavior, but I would not be surprised to find that Chauvin’s actions were nothing unusual at Minneapolis PD.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: Why did Trump have his school records sealed? Trump for 60 years claimed to be Swedish then all of a sudden with German Chancellor Angela Merckel he said he’s German. What is his real ancestry? Was he really born in the U.S.?
Answer: Trump’s father was German; his mother was Scottish. Dad told many people he was Swedish in order to avoid anti-German bias around Word War II. Trump has also claimed to be Swedish. His school records are another thing entirely. Trump has boasted numerous times of his genius, his athletic prowess, and his general success in all things. One of his professors at Wharton described Trump as “the dumbest student I ever had.” Trump claimed to have made the Dean’s List on several occasions,. The Dean’s List is published and archived, and Trump’s name never appeared on it. If Trump’s transcripts were released, they would reflect that he was a marginal student on his best days and just squeaked out of school, mostly because his father endowed the school with a lot of money.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: How are police challenge coins used within police departments and among officers?
Answer: Challenge coins are used in two principal ways: recognition and membership. A chief of police might make an appearance in roll call to “coin” an officer for an exceptional bit of work. There will be some record of the incident in the officer’s personnel file, but this makes the event a more public one where his peers also see what the chief recognizes as desirable behavior. Secondly, an officer might be given a challenge coin after completing an especially difficult training course or at the conclusion of a tour with an elite subunit of the department. Officers could receive a coin after finishing an assignment at motorcycle school, a narcotics investigation unit, a training stint as an instructor, or some other laudable activity.

Question: Is it normal for a cop to write a ticket for illegal parking when the vehicle is broken down on an interstate entrance ramp?
Answer: Issuing a parking ticket for the broken-down vehicle is the way some agencies start following abandoned vehicles in their databases. The ticket is automatically flagged so that someone can be sent to tow the vehicle if it’s still there after three days or whatever the grace period is.

Question: Does the Federal Bureau of Investigation which is a federal law enforcement agency do protection details for anybody other than the FBI Director and Attorney General regularly like when US Marshals protected Trump era Education Secretary Betsy Devos?
Answer: There are protective details for senior FBI officials, such as assistant directors. The FBI does not handle protective details for people outside their agency.

Question: When a candidate runs for president of the USA, are they subjected to any IQ or psychological test?
Answer: No. The Constitution spells out the qualifications to be President, and they didn’t know about psychometric tests then.

Question: What is the reality behind Sheriffs being able to swear in regular private citizens as deputys to help with law enforcement emergencies? Was this ever a real thing or just another case of Hollywood make believe?
Answer: That was really the law in most states, although those laws have been mostly stricken from the books. A sheriff was empowered to conscript able-bodied men to give chase to fugitives and otherwise assist him in keeping the peace. The assembled body of conscripts was called the sheriff’s “posse.” Many sheriffs still have a posse. This is often an honorary group of horsemen who ride in parades and otherwise get to dress up like Old West lawmen a few times a year. Sometimes they are involved in fund-raising for special programs of the sheriff’s office.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: Where in the state of Nevada would I sue either the police officer or city for depriving me of due process of law? Would I sue the officer individualy or the city he represents? Would the venue be justice court or district court?
Answer: Cops are generally sued in both their professional and personal capacity. The defendants usually include the city or county, the agency, and even the chief of police or sheriff. I’ve never heard of one of these being filed in Justice Court. District Court in Nevada is the court of general jurisdiction. You will need an attorney to file this lawsuit. If you want the lawyer to take the case on contingency (where his fees are paid out of a judgement or award, not up front), you’ll have to convince him that it’s worth some money. Most cases like this aren’t.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: Is there a way to have a warrant served in NC without turning yourself in and getting arrested? Can you hire a lawyer to have the warrant served for you?
Answer: An attorney may be able to arrange for bail to be posted and forfeited on the offense, ending the matter. If the charge is very serious and requires an appearance before the court, the lawyer may be able to arrange for bond to be posted, so that when you appear in court, you don’t have to be in custody.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: How do salaries for firefighters and paramedics differ from that for police officers?
Answer: In cities and counties with paid/career law enforcement officers and firefighters (most U.S. firefighters are volunteers), salaries are roughly comparable. When the firefighters get a raise, the cops will usually catch up within a year or two. EMTs and paramedics who are not firefighters or cops are generally paid less. An EMT in New York City makes less than half what a firefighter does.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: How can a law enforcement officer keep his job if he’s married and having an affair? Is there a code of conduct/ethics that can jeopardize his job?
Answer: Few law enforcement agencies regulate the marital conduct of their officers. A few in religiously conservative states like Idaho (heavily Mormon) do have policies in place, because adultery is forbidden by state law. 32-604. Adultery. Adultery is the voluntary sexual intercourse of a married person with a person other than the offender’s husband or wife. Fornication (sexual intercourse between two unmarried people) was outlawed in Idaho some years back. I remember that a young woman was charged and convicted or fornication, but her male partner was not.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: Why didn't the other police officers pull Derek Chauvin off of George Floyd when they saw that he'd stop breathing?
Answer: Derek Chauvin was a very senior officer, and the three cops who were with him were very junior. The organizational culture of many law enforcement agencies holds that seniority is everything. A rookie officer never challenges a senior officer, even if the senior is doing something that appears to be wrong. Minneapolis PD and other agencies now include training in their academies to the effect that officers have a duty to intervene when something bad is happening, no matter how disparate the time on the job. Every cop I know who watched the Chauvin video was saying, “Get off his neck.” Kneeling on someone’s shoulder or neck momentarily is a valid restraint technique with a resistive suspect you’re trying to handcuff. George Floyd was wasted on marijuana and fentanyl. He was in poor health to begin with. He wasn’t capable of offering much resistance. Chauvin had three cops to help him if Floyd had been resistive to handcuffing. Chauvin should have cuffed Floyd, sat him up, and probably called for an ambulance. Organizational culture can overrule a policy manual or standard of training. It’s difficult to change.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: How can a person be sentenced as a habitual offender for only being arrested and charged with a felony one time in the state they live, but had a felony charge in another state and served their time for that charge?
Answer: Convictions are cumulative. You don’t get to reset the counter by moving to another state. Your criminal history is recorded on the Interstate Identification Index run by the FBI every time you’re fingerprinted. Every cop and court officer has access to that record. When you’re charged, the prosecutor is going to count up your arrests and convictions and file a habitual offender package on you if your record will sustain it. A few states ignore any charges that are more than 20 years old, but most states have an unlimited “lookback” period to count prior offenses. In your case, that means this situation only gets worse with time if you continue to commit crimes, no matter where you commit them. Unless you have an ambition to become an expert on the comparative quality of prison systems in multiple states, I’d suggest reevaluating your life choices.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: Is a person guilty of an alleged crime they've been charged with, such as shoplifting, if there was no motive or intent, but just a freak occurrence that can be explained?
Answer: I’m not sure how a shoplifting incident can be a “freak occurrence.” Did a rogue wave wash ashore and direct a carton of cigarettes into your pants? You are free to offer nearly any defense to shoplifting you like, but the state is permitted to cross-examine you. That’s usually where the “freak occurrence” defenses come apart. A judge is going to be more lenient to someone who comes clean and admits their crime than with someone who assumes the court is so dumb the offender can get a fantastic story by them.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: Can cops cut off your clothes if I refuse a strip search or change to prison clothes?
Answer: They’ll try to remove the clothes without destroying them, as they want you to have something to wear when you’re released. One way or another, you’re going to be wearing the jail uniform. If you refuse to put it on, you’ll be held in a bare cell naked until you decide to get with the program. Lots of people go into jail thinking they’re not going to bend to the will of their captives. No one leaves thinking that.

Question: Could a guy that was diagnosed with autism and had learning disability in school get accepted into the police force or any opportunity at all in law enforcement?
Answer: Possibly. Autism is a “spectrum” disorder, with Rain Man types at one end and people who are just socially awkward at the other. Question: If I apply to be a new police officer and get a job, would I have any say in where they put me? For instance, if I wanted to be assigned to the airport, would they take that into consideration?
Answer: As a rookie officer, you generally get zero input into your assignment. In a general-service police department, you’re almost certainly going to be assigned to uniformed patrol. After a few years, you may have the opportunity to apply for other assignments. Airport patrol is usually reserved for senior officers who have chosen to get out of the weather and don’t want a lot of activity. I occasionally worked an overtime shift at the airport, and its saving grace was that it was easy money. There were two of us per shift, sometimes augmented by a sergeant. One would stand at the security checkpoint podium for an hour, ready to assist the security folks (pre-TSA) when needed. The most common incident was when someone would come through the checkpoint with pepper spray in their baggage. That was a chargeable crime, but we would offer them a pass if they simply surrendered the pepper spray. Now and then, someone would refuse, and they would go to jail. 99% gave up the pepper spray canister, and we had a fill-in-the-blanks report to cover it. The pepper spray went into a bin that was periodically sent to hazardous waste management. The only time I looked, there were over a hundred cans of pepper spray in there. When one cop was at the podium, the other could do just about anything they wanted so long as they were available to respond or assist with an incident. Some went to the office and napped. A friend with a more recent assignment there watched movies on DVD. If you were really bored, you could do foot patrol around the concourses, or go eat lunch. You generally had to be very senior to get the airport gig. Like I said, it was easy money. If you’re really anxious to work at an airport, apply to airports where they have their own police. They don’t have any other assignments.

Question: How do you know if you are going to fail an EtG urine alcohol test? I’m looking for a reliable calculator. I had 2 drinks in one hour on Wednesday and test 47 hours later.

If you’re risking jail or other legal consequences by consuming alcohol, you should give serious consideration to the notion that you may be an alcoholic and addicted to alcohol. The only way to recover from alcoholism is to stop drinking. Believe it or not, people get through their whole lives without consuming alcohol. It doesn’t have to be a driving force of your life.

Question: If I apply to be a police officer as a new recruit after I get accepted, will I have to go to a police academy or will I straight start work?
Answer: Different agencies have different procedures. My employer had an in-house academy for the entire time I worked there (they now train new hires at a regional academy). Starting with my class in 1979, our first day on the payroll was our first day in the academy. On completion of the academy, we moved to field training on the street. Half of the class of the previous academy had been working the street with a training officer for six to nine months before they started the academy. This procedure would be regarded as too high-risk now. I doubt anyone but the smallest departments (especially in Louisiana, where they play kind of fast and loose with training requirements) engage in that practice now. If you enroll at a regional academy as a “free agent,” not on any department’s payroll and without the promise of a job on completion, on graduation you have to market yourself to area agencies as an academy grad ready to begin field training. Many parts of the country have a glut of academy grads who will never find jobs. Unless they work as volunteer reserve officers, their academy certifications will eventually expire and if they get hired anywhere, they have to complete another academy. Getting hired by an agency that puts you through the academy is by far your best bet, even if you have to move to that area to take the job. Once you’re certified and off probation, you can apply as a lateral hire to an agency where you really want to work, and have a much better chance of getting the job. The outfits that first hire you hate it when their recruits fly the coop after training, but there’s not much they can do about it. LAPD used to sue recruits for training costs who left within the first five years for other agencies, but they got sued themselves over the practice, and had to stop.

Question: Are police allowed to patrol neighborhoods randomly with K-9 units? This seems like a 4th amendment violation or at best walking the line.
Answer: I don’t think you understand the Fourth Amendment. The Fourth Amendment protects citizens against unreasonable searches. A search, under the Fourth Amendment, is a government intrusion into a reasonable expectation of privacy. For a search to be reasonable, it must be supported by probable cause. Probable cause is the reasonable belief that a search will reveal evidence of a crime. When a police officer applies for a search warrant, he lays his probable cause before a judge and asks, in essence, “Is this enough?” If the judge agrees that it is, he signs the search warrant and the officer can go forward to search the premises described in the warrant. If the officer makes a warrantless search, he gambles that his probable cause, once presented in court, will be judged as adequate to sustain the search. If the probable cause is insufficient, then the fruits of the search (whatever evidence was obtained) are excluded from consideration at trial. A K9 officer driving around a neighborhood has no special abilities to intrude into any reasonable expectations of privacy. If he does happen on a suspicious situation where he believes evidence of a crime can be found, and if that evidence is something his dog can detect (such as the odor of contraband drugs), he may decide to have the dog sniff the area. So long as the dog and handler are in a place where they have a right to be, such as the side of the road, there is no Fourth Amendment violation. If that open air sniff causes the handler to believe there are drugs or other contraband inside a vehicle, a backpack, or whatever other object was sniffed, he may have probable cause to make a more intrusive search. Your question reminds of the countless protests of people in the field who have watched a few YouTube videos and decided they are experts on search and seizure law. This is a complex area of law that changes constantly, and most attorneys will admit they are seldom up to date with the latest changes unless they have researched the topic recently. Shouting, “This is a violation of my Fourth Amendment rights!” does not make a valid constitutional argument. The cops almost always know more about these laws than you do, and they know not to violate them, because to do so means losing the evidence and the case they’re attached to.

Question: Do LAPD officers make enough money to afford living in Los Angeles with a family?

That’s probably enough to finance a rented house or apartment and pay reasonable living expenses. The average home purchase price in Los Angeles County is just short of $900K, so most officers won’t be able to purchase a home there without substantial help from a third party, such as a parent gifting their down payment. Many LAPD officers live well outside the county and commute, but that doesn’t help that much, given California home prices. I don’t see this situation changing. The City of Los Angeles would have to double or triple the police pay rate to give the cops a shot at buying a house in LA County, and the city could never afford that. One solution that has worked in some other cities is for the city to either buy distressed properties or build homes designated for sale to police officers. Given the homeless situation in LA, I think this would be a politically unpopular move.

Question: What are the benefits of being a police officer rather than a firefighter?
Answer: The pay, benefits, and pension tend to be about the same. Firefighters have their own fraternity or brotherhood, but it’s distinct from that of the cops. The biggest difference, I think, is that the cop’s job doesn’t end when he goes off duty. He may go off the clock, but he’s likely still carrying his badge and firearm, and may have handcuffs or other police tools with him. He feels the need to be able to react as a police officer should he find himself in a tense situation. Firefighters don’t carry an off-duty axe or Halligan tool (although I have seen some with huge fire extinguishers in their personal cars), and other than the need to perform first aid in some cases, they have no special obligations (official or self-imposed) when they’re off duty. Carrying the gun is a big deal. Most cops experiment with different ways of carrying their gun off duty, and within a few years, have an entire drawer or two full of holsters they tried and discarded. They feel naked if they leave the house without the gun. Having the gun 24/7 also has a high CDI (Chicks Dig It) factor. I got a lot more girls while I was a cop than I did before I was one. I don’t include my post-cop years in that equation, as I was married then. Although one’s police powers generally extended only to the borders of the state where the officer is commissioned, for many years there was a kind of Code of the West practice that an out-of-state cop would not be hassled for carrying his gun so long as he behaved himself. In 2004, this practice was codified in the law with the Law Enforcement Officers Safety Act, and active duty cops could carry their firearms in every state. The privilege is also extended to retired cops with ten years or more of service, providing they qualify with the firearms once a year. Where I live, the local Fraternal Order of Police chapter puts on a qualification session (actually, it takes a couple of days to get everyone through) for retired folks, even ones like me from other states. Thanks to them, I don’t have to feel naked when I leave the house. I may not be a cop anymore, but the awareness of danger never leaves you.

Question: How hard is it to be hired to a police department and sent to the academy? The one I want to work for is currently full. I turn 21 in 28 days. What are the odds a position opens up?
Answer: Much depends on your qualifications. The job market for cops is very good right now. Most agencies have openings. The problem is with finding suitable recruits. Many applicants have inadequate academic preparation (they can’t write a coherent report or do simple math), use prescription drugs like Adderall, are obese and/or in poor physical condition. The military has the same problem in finding recruits, as only about 25% of the similar cohort (men and women 17–25) are fit for military service. It’s relatively unusual to be hired as a cop at age 21. Few people are mature enough for the job at that age. A successful term of military service can often accelerate the maturation process. If you were to be hired, it’s unlikely that it would happen in the space of four weeks. The hiring cycle for law enforcement can take a year or more. The biggest time hog is often the background investigation, which requires interviews with people who knew you at different stages of life. You might feel pressure to become a cop as close to your 21st birthday as possible, but no one else will. Most agencies will want to see you grow up a bit.

Question: In Nevada, pulled over for no plates, never suspected of being impaired, not arrested, not tested on the scene, left scene by ambulance, can police use tests at hospital to later charge you without told suspected DUI?

Question: What is a circumstances a judge will look back 20 years on a DUI if the states wash out is 10 years?
Answer: If the lookback period is seven years, DUI convictions during that time may be used to enhance the sentence for the instant case. Question: What happens after someone is arrested and taken to the police station, and how many days later do they go to court (if they happen to go to the court)?
Answer: If the jail and the police station are the same place, the prisoner is booked (photographed and fingerprinted) into jail, showered and given a jail uniform, and assigned to a cell or bunk. Unless there are some unusual circumstances like a natural disaster, they are supposed to go before a judge within 48 hours of booking. There, they will be formally advised of the charges filed against them and asked to enter a plea. If they plead guilty and the charges are minor, they may be released on time served. They may also be given a fine and released, the fine to be paid later (many of them won’t be). With more major charges, a guilty plea might mean a pre-sentence investigation before sentencing. If the prisoner can’t post bail, they stay in custody. The PSI might take a month. If the prisoner pleads not guilty, the judge will ask the prosecutor for a bail recommendation, which the defense or the prisoner may agree to or object to. Either way, the decision on whether to grant bail and what the bail will be is up to the judge. The judge will also set a date for a pre-trial hearing or a trial, depending on local custom. The trial date might be months away.

Question: Does it take a lot more intelligence to be a detective than the police?
Answer: First, detectives are the police. A detective is just a uniformed police officer who has an assignment other than uniformed patrol. TV detectives tend to act like exalted royalty among “uniforms,” but at most places the relationship is far more congenial. I regularly worked with detectives who had been my trainees when they were rookies. One got kind of full of himself. He was well-connected in the department and got an assignment to narcotics shortly after completing probation. One night, I and another patrol officer were assigned to assist the narcs with serving several search warrants. We went in first, so anyone inside would know it was the real police and not pretenders. We had parked our patrol cars and ridden to the search warrant venues in the narcs’ unmarked van. When we were all done, my former rookie asked his supervisor, “Sarge, you want me to take the uniforms back to their cars?” I interrupted the conversation to say, “Officer ______, did you just refer to your former field training officer as a ‘uniform?”” There was an uncomfortable pause before he answered, “Yes, sir. Sorry, sir.” He called me “sir” for about a year afterward. I worked with some detectives who were unquestionably smart people, and others who had to concentrate to remember how to grunt. The same was true of uniformed patrol officers, as that was where everyone started. Assignments to detectives had a lot more to do with one political connections and standing than with IQ points. In fact, my agency had three card-carrying members of Mensa while I worked there. We were all uniformed patrol officers. Many questions I get on Quora come from people who believe they can be hired into law enforcement and immediately start work as a detective. Doesn’t happen. You may luck out or be well-connected and get an early detective assignment, but it’s more likely you’ll work in uniformed patrol, chasing the radio and taking reports, for five to ten years before you get a shot at detectives. And, whether you do or not doesn’t have a lot to do with your IQ.

Question: Does the higher number on a police officer badge represent a higher rank?
Answer: The meaning or significance of a badge number is different from one agency to another. In Oregon, all law enforcement officers are trained by the Oregon Dept. of Public Safety Standards & Training (DPSST), and everyone is assigned a DPSST number. it’s common for agencies to assign the officer’s DPSST number to their badge, which is how you see officers in 15-man agencies with five-digit badge numbers. A lower badge number means that officer entered law enforcement before those with higher numbers, as the numbers are issued sequentially. At LAPD, the badge number is mainly for inventory purposes. The number officers place on their reports and others identify themselves is their serial number, which is not the same as the badge number. An officer with a LAPD ancestor might ask to have the same badge number his grandfather or uncle had. When I was hired at Reno PD in 1979, only non-supervisors had badge numbers. Badges were issued from a pool of numbers that I think went like this: Detectives: 1–50 Police Officers: 51–299 Jailers: 300–399 Auxiliary/Volunteer Officers: 400–499 When someone left, their badge number went back into the pool (the employee usually kept the badge itself, so a new one was made). I was issued Badge #138. Later on, for complicated reasons, I was given #291. Then the department decided to give everyone an employee number that for the incumbents was based on your Social Security number. I thought issuing them in order of seniority would have made more sense, but no one asked me. An officer from New York (low SSN) got #0001, and I (from California, high SSN) got #1111. The department was too cheap to re-issue badges with the four-digit numbers on them, so everyone wore the badge they had been issued until they left the agency. New hires were issued employee numbers based on hiring sequence and that number was engraved on their badge. The badge number became an indicator of seniority. A higher badge number there indicates a more recent hire. If an employee is promoted, they keep the same number, but they get a new badge with the new rank on it. The rank of the officer usually appears on the badge. When I was hired, police officers had no indication of rank on their badge (this has since changed). A banner over the top of the badge would say “SERGEANT,” “LIEUTENANT” or whatever.

Question: Is it true that you need to do a court order before you can get your fingerprints and photo removed from the database?
Answer: Probably, and you might not be successful. Most criminal justice systems maintain or use multiple information databases. There might be one for Anytown PD, another for all the agencies in the bi- or tri-county Anytown area, a state-level database, and the Big Kahuna, the National Criminal Information Center, aka NCIC. NCIC is owned and operated by the FBI. If you have been fingerprinted by a law enforcement agency, your prints and associated data are in all of those systems. You often have to petition each one to delete your records, and give them a good reason why they should do it. Say you get a court order to expunge your records from the kindly old Justice of the Peace in Anytown. The Anytown PD will probably comply. Don’t count on that being a total erasure. There will still be cops who remember the case, and there may be some reports that reference it. It’s all but impossible to chase this stuff down 100%. The regional and state databases might go along, but it’s an even bet they’ll tell you to get your order from a higher court. You’ll have to convince a judge in the court of general jurisdiction that it is in the public interest to purge your prints. That might be a tough sell. Where you’re really going to get pushback is from the FBI. They’ll tell you the state court has no jurisdiction over a federal agency (and they will be correct). You can try and get an order from a federal court, but don’t be surprised if you are shot down. How does having those prints in the system affect you? Unless you continue on a life of crime, there will likely be zero impact. My prints and mug shot have been in the system since 1968, when I had a summer job with the city where I grew up (good luck trying to recognize me today from that mug shot). I have since been printed many times, as I have been a public employee most of my life and those jobs required being fingerprinted. The only time it had any effect at all was a few years ago when I applied for a Known Traveler Number with the TSA. The KTN allows me to use the TSA PreCheck line at the airport and get through security faster. I was told the KTN would come through a little faster if my prints were already in the system. I had the KTN two days later. On the other end of the spectrum, say that you get printed for whatever minor crime you did, and the prints remain in the system. Twenty years from now, your latent print is developed off of a flash drive or whatever data storage device people will be using then, and the flash drive contains child pornography. The police will be looking to have an up close and personal chat with you. I suggest you bring a lawyer.

Question: Do you consider a cop receiving free meals or other low value gifts, given solely because the person is a police officer to be corruption or not? Why?
Answer: This topic is of special interest to me, because it was the subject of my master’s thesis in 1986. The thesis was edited and published in Journal of Police Science and Administration in March 1988. There was a time when police officers very seldom paid for their food while they were working. Furnishing the beat cop with dinner was considered a kind of community support. Refinements that made the practice a bit more iffy came to appear. In some places. the cop could have only one pre-designated item, usually something that was moving slowly that day. If the cop didn’t like that item, or wanted something else, the business owner got irritated. The cop might not get charged for the special meal, but it would be of lower quality, like with too much fat or served cold when it was supposed to be hot. My field training officer (FTO) took it on himself to teach me the rules of free meals around downtown Reno. At one place, you could have anything you wanted, but they didn't want cops coming in between the hours of 1700–1900, which were their peak meal times. At another place, cops could have anything on the left side of the menu, which was sandwiches and salads. The right side of the menu, all full, multi-course dinners, was available at half the listed menu price. There were similar policies at most restaurants. I endured an embarrassing incident with my FTO and sergeant, who usually ate with us. The restaurant, part of a casino, had coffee shop-style fare, with some added Chinese dishes. I usually had their soup and sandwich special, which was something like $2.50 menu price in 1979 (my starting salary then was $13,500 per year). The sergeant would almost always order a steak, which was around $7.00. The food was normally free for cops, with a cash tip left for the server. One day, the server brought us all checks for the full menu price. She explained, “Sorry guys—the casino manager said the comps were getting to be too much, so we have to charge you guys now.” I got out my wallet and laid $5 on the table. The sergeant stood up, and loud enough to be heard on the street outside, shouted, “WHERE THE F*** IS THAT CASINO MANAGER? I WANT TO SEE HIS ASS RIGHT F***ING NOW!” There was a brief and heated conversation (I was so mortified that I offered to pay for everyone’s meal), and the sergeant announced that the casino would henceforth be off limits to police officers. He did not have the authority to do this, and in fact nothing happened. Police officers and firefighters could see movies for free. The rationale explained to me was that cops and firefighters are trained in first aid and CPR, and that showing their insurance company that we were often on scene would reduce their liability insurance rates. I found this specious, as the theater folks would have difficulty identifying and locating us in a dark theater if we were needed, but the practice was still that the display of a badge, along with signing a log at the ticket booth, got you in for free. When I started questioning the practice of accepting gratuities and refused to take them while I was working, it caused some dissension among my fellow officers. They often took the position that I was a do-gooder, trying to ruin a good thing for them. This created a bit of practical joke-style subterfuge. If those movie theater logs still exist, you could review the records from the early-to-mid eighties and find that I saw virtually every movie released to Reno theaters during that time, sometimes attending multiple showings all at the same time. Everyone used my badge number and name. The questionable aspect of the practice, absent any actual attempt at favoritism or quid pro quo, is that the conditions of the gratuity are seldom discussed at the time it is given. Does the giver expect special treatment if they are ever on the end of an enforcement action? Some fast food restaurants ask for the officer’s badge number, which gets coded onto the receipt for the food. In other places, the officer is asked to sign the receipt with the name and badge number. I read about a restaurant owner who got a traffic ticket and was assessed a fine. He brought in a shoebox of hundreds of signed receipts for free food given to cops, and told the judge, “I think I’ve paid enough already.” The fine was dismissed. The practice of accepting gratuities is declining, and is outlawed in some parts of the country. Still some cops regard it as their birthright, and get very testy at the suggestion that they pay for their food while they’re working.

Answer: Depending on the depth of a background investigation, I doubt there are very many people who can remember all the details of their history. I know that last can be a challenge for some people, especially if they were staying with friends or were in some other transient state. I once applied for a federal law enforcement/special agent position. The background investigation form was thirteen pages long, and that was without supplements for information that wouldn’t fit into the form blanks. I was supposed to list every place I had ever lived, every school I had ever attended, every job I had ever held, and along with this who my neighbors, teachers, supervisors, etc. were. This was a challenge, as my family was poor and we moved from rental to rental every few years while I was growing up. My high school was the thirteenth school I had attended. I had an itinerant job history, especially right after I graduated from college and was doing just about anything to remain solvent. I rented an IBM Selectric typewriter so the print on the form would be as pristine as possible, and worked on the form every day for three weeks. I wish I had kept a copy around, as that was probably the most complete history I had ever assembled (don’t make my mistake and trash it). I wasn’t offered the job. Had I gotten a conditional offer, I would have been subject to a polygraph to verify everything, or at least my recall of it. I had to undergo a similar background investigation and polygraph when I became a police officer (the polygraph operator remarked at the end of the exam that I was “the most boring person I have ever examined”), but this was far more in depth. So, depending on what you’re asked, do the best you can, and say “I don’t remember” if you don’t. Make some effort to fill in the blanks by calling people and looking up addresses. Above all, DO NOT LIE. Don’t try to conceal anything on a background investigation. If you do, and your lie is discovered, the background investigator will wonder what else you lied about that he didn’t find. You will be done.

Question: When the police come to your home to ask for security footage for an incident that took place out in the street, (you weren’t involved in) they always demand you identify yourself. Are you required to do so?
Answer: No. The “demand” (is asking a question like “May I have your name?” a “demand?”) is simply a way of documenting where the video footage originated, should there be any litigation concerning it. If you refused to answer, the police would find some other method of identifying you. If this took place at your residence, it wouldn’t be all that hard. If the matter goes to trial and the video is used at trial, the state is required to “lay a foundation” for the introduction of the evidence. That requires naming the time, place, and who supplied the footage. If that comes to pass, you won’t have a choice about identifying yourself. You’ll be issued a subpoena requiring you to appear, and when you’re asked your name, you must respond truthfully or be held in contempt. The only way you could refuse that question is if your name could incriminate you, e.g. it turns out you’ve been hiding out when you were placed on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted List. If that turns out to be the case, the video evidence will be the least of your worries.

Question: How can PennDOT force you to have an ignition interlock after you serve a year suspension for refusal and beat the DUI case?
Answer: I’m not familiar with Pennsylvania law, so this is speculation based on the way other states operate. I’m going to guess that you refused a blood or breath test when you were arrested. That carries its own civil penalties outside of any criminal consequences for the DUI itself. Your driver’s license is automatically suspended or revoked for the implied consent refusal, and I’m guessing that Pennsylvania law then requires you to install an ignition interlock on your car and keep it in place for a preset period. Your driver’s license can reinstated once the original revocation period has run, but it’s valid only if you have the ignition interlock installed on whatever vehicle you are driving (if you own two cars, you can’t put the interlock on one and drive the other). If the fees in Pennsylvania are anything like they are here, be prepared for some sticker shock. I was in a car stereo shop that had a license to install and maintain the interlock devices. They had a price list of services posted. Installation and maintenance of the interlock cost well over $1000 per year, and that was if nothing went wrong. People are forever trying to tamper with the interlocks, and that causes them to lock up and throw an error code. It’s back to the stereo shop for a maintenance visit with a preset fee amount. Have you considered just giving up driving after you have been drinking? That is 100% effective in avoiding DUI charges.

Question: Why do people think cops are there to protect and serve? They aren't. I have caught local police lying through their teeth multiple times.
Answer: I won’t pretend to tell you that cops are all Boy Scouts and never lie, because I’ve known some I wouldn’t trust to fetch my newspaper. However, these were in the very small minority, and most of them eventually got fired (the rest promoted to management). Some years back when body cameras were just coming onto the market, the Las Vegas Metro Police did a pilot project with one of their patrol districts. All the cops wore body cameras and recorded most of their police-citizen encounters. The recordings became an integral part of misconduct complaints against officers. Better than 90% of the time, the recording proved that the complainant was lying about the officer’s conduct, and the officer was exonerated. In most of the remaining cases, the evidence was either equivocal or the alleged misconduct could be explained in a context that showed the officer had acted properly, given the circumstances at the time. For example, the complaint might be based on knowledge that was not available to the officer at the time of the incident. The officer couldn’t be blamed for not knowing something that wouldn’t be revealed until later. Whenever I hear a complaint like yours, I have to wonder how you have so many contacts with the police where the officers are engaging in misconduct. I’ve lived in the same medium-size (~84,000 people) city for 24 years, and the only contacts I’ve had with the local police were when I went to the police station for something (well, I have lunch with a police sergeant now and then, but I don’t count that). I’ve never been pulled over or detained for investigation. Some people don’t seem to be able to get through a week without some adverse contact with the police. If you keep having bad experiences with the police, and it’s not the exact same officer, maybe you should stop blaming the variables and look closer at the constant.

Question: Have you ever found more than $20 on the street?
Answer: When I was in college, I was riding my bike and found a checkbook lying in the street near campus. There was around $80 in it, along with the blank checks. The address on the checks was about three miles away. I rode my bike to the residence and knocked on the door. I asked the man who answered, “Are you [name on checks]?” and he replied that he was. I handed him the checkbook. Had I suddenly burst into flame, I don't think he could have been more surprised. He was also a student at the same college, figured he had lost the checkbook somewhere around campus, and never thought he would see it again. He glanced quickly at the portion where the money was, but didn’t count it. I suppose he figured I would return all of it or none of it. He offered me $5 out of the checkbook (he didn't appear any more prosperous than me, although I suspect he had a car and I didn’t), but I told him that was my good deed for today. I hope he paid it forward some day.

Question: Criminal justice: in the united states, people have to right to remain silent when they are question by police. in your opinion, is this a good law?

It’s exactly what they hated about criminal investigations under the King. Very few people avail themselves of the Fourth Amendment. Most of them think they can talk their way out of trouble. The police love this.

Question: How does the FBI handle homicide cases the states fail to solve?
Answer: The FBI handles very few homicide cases, although popular entertainment media might suggest otherwise. The FBI might step in if there were multiple murders that crossed state borders, but when all the killings reside in one state, federal involvement is likely to be limited to creating a profile of the suspect if the locals are out of investigative leads. The profile would not be done with a team of mismatched agents on a bizjet, but rather by a team of agents who work out of the basement of the FBI Academy in Quantico and have law enforcement “customers” come to them. If a murder case gets to be beyond the investigative capacity of whatever local agency first got the report, then it’s usually passed to the state’s investigative agency. This may be a part of the state police or highway patrol, or a separate agency, such as the Kansas Bureau of Investigation or the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension. Most states have some type of investigative agency.

Question: The vaccine for covid was actually worser than the virus itself. Do people not realize that? Both the government and the vaccine companies need to be sued for forcing everyone to take this poison.

Question: Can a criminal record for a misdemeanor, a gross misdemeanor, or a felony conviction from one state be legally held against you in another state?
