Question: What makes a cop have the right to impound a car for not having your DL on them but gives the DL number?
Answer: I’ve never understood the problem people have with carrying their drivers license when they drive. You’re required to carry the physical license. A few states are experimenting with digital licenses, but we’re mostly not there yet. Besides, what is easier to carry, a small card that weighs a few grams, or a much larger electronic device? People won’t go to the bathroom without their phone, but they can’t be bothered to carry their license. I lost track of the times I was told, “I don’t have my license, but you can run it.” I can? Oh, I just love doing that! Why can’t you be bothered to carry the damn thing? Anyone can memorize your drivers license number and give it to a cop. If they’re close to your physical description, they can pass as you. They can get cited or arrested under your name. This is harder if you carry your drivers license. To get back to your original question, if you’re not carrying your license, you’re not supposed to drive. Your vehicle can be impounded until you produce a licensed driver, and that means someone with a physical license on them.

Question: Should everyone have an ID card?
Answer: I think it’s a good idea, despite the “Big Brother” implications. An ID card demonstrates who you are, but more importantly, it demonstrates who you aren’t. If you look like Joe Sixpack, currently wanted for six gruesome murders, and whose photo is on every cop’s clipboard, you might find yourself detained frequently and inconveniently while the locals figure out you’re not Joe. If you choose not to carry identification because, by God, this is America and you have a Constitutional right to wander around without so much as a nickel in your pockets, good for you. Enjoy your time handcuffed in the prisoner cage of the patrol car while we try and find some way to ensure we’re not letting a serial killer walk down the road. I walk around my neighborhood every night for exercise. I’ve never been stopped. Maybe my reflective vest (prevention against becoming a road pizza) and my German shepherd indicate to any passing cops, whom I very rarely see, that I’m not a prowler or a burglar. However, my ID is always in my pocket, and if I was stopped, I would present it without hesitation. I haven’t got any outstanding arrest warrants or protective orders, and I don’t especially care if they know who I am or where I live. If they wanted confirmation, I’d take them to my house and make them a cup of coffee. But, that’s just me.

Question: When did law enforcement begin using weapon mounted lights on their firearms?

If you’re searching an area where you might expect there to be a deadly threat, a pistol-mounted light is useful, as it frees up one hand that would otherwise be carrying a flashlight. If you’re just looking for something in a dark place, the gun belongs in your holster.

Question: What job can I get with a bachelor’s degree that is best for creative and artistic minds that pays at least 75k a year? I’m looking into college but I don’t know what path I should take.
Answer: Let’s see…in my last full-time editor job, which entailed a fair amount of expository writing, I made $70,000. I got $60,000 in a similar job just before that. Both of those jobs were, at the time, the most money I had ever made. Prior to that, I was a community college professor, making (I think) about $35,000 per year. I should add those jobs came around after 20+ years of criminal justice experience (I was working for a police website) and 15 years of writing for law enforcement publications freelance at $75-$300 per article. The notion that I would have gotten those jobs at any salary right out of college was laughable. Without considerable experience and an established “rep,” the only jobs I can think of where you are likely to make anywhere near your goal right out of college are certain STEM fields (mostly engineering) and sales. Good salesmen are seldom unemployed. They tend to be driven by money, not artistic expression. They live in a somewhat depressing world of “no.” They might get a hundred “nos” before they get to a “yes.” They live for the “yesses.” They have to be incredibly resilient. I tried that once, and found it was so not for me. I’m afraid you have a cruel dose of reality waiting in your future. You can maybe find a job where you can express yourself creatively, but it’s unlikely to pay a lot of money. You have to decide whether artistic expression or filthy lucre is more important to you. If you do take the creative path, you’ll likely work for years in low-paying, unrewarding jobs before you find one that suits your creative needs. Hollywood and New York City are both full of actors, dancers, screenwriters and playwrights who are waiting tables and parking cars, trying to live their dream. Most of them won’t make it. It’s a cold world. Be prepared to face it.

Question: What can make my drug test for felony probation negative if I smoke two blunt 3 days separate?
Answer: Not smoking blunts or using any other marijuana product. You don’t seem to be getting the idea behind your probation and its restrictions. My guess is that your drug and/or alcohol use has something to do with why you got into trouble in the first place. Your conditions of probation include refraining from use of marijuana, any illegal drugs, and possibly alcohol. If you use these things, you are in violation and the court can revoke your probation. That could mean going to jail, where it will be much more difficult to obtain marijuana. That you are risking violating your probation tells me you have an addictive problem with marijuana. Yes, I know that marijuana is not supposed to be addictive. I also know that people go to incredible lengths to obtain it when doing so puts them at considerable risk. That tells me they have an unhealthy relationship with the drug. Your probation officer deals with an entire class of people who are trying to hide their illegal conduct, including their drug use. They have seen and heard every possible attempt and method of beating the drug tests. They know how to compensate for the subterfuge. It is unlikely you are going to fool them. I suggest you come clean about your drug use, then make a sincere effort to abstain from using marijuana. If you can’t imagine doing that, then, well, enjoy jail.

Question: How do I find an attorney in New Jersey that handles personal injury/slander (federal)? The case is in Montana.
Answer: If you have a case in Montana, you’re going to need a lawyer who practices in Montana. You are unlikely to find an attorney licensed in both states who is willing to jet back and forth across the country on your behalf. I assume you are looking for an attorney who will take your case on contingency or pro bono. This is also unlikely. Unless they work for a large law firm, attorneys are small businessmen. They look for cases that will generate income. They will occasionally take a case on contingency (meaning they get paid roughly one-third of any award if you/they prevail), but most of the cases people bring to them are unlikely to result in any significant damage award. In a personal injury/slander case, you would have to first identify a responsible party with enough assets to make it worthwhile to sue them, and show monetary damages to yourself. Being really pissed off at someone who done you wrong doesn’t qualify. Of course, if you have, say, $50,000 lying around that you can pay an attorney as a retainer, you can probably have your pick of lawyers. But, if you had that, you probably wouldn’t be asking about this on Quora.

Question: Can you get charged for DUI if you were walking up to your apartment?
Answer: If the officer could provide testimony to “put you behind the wheel” of your car, yes. Hypothetical scenario: you’re driving home from the bar. An officer sees you weaving out of your traffic lane or otherwise driving in a way that indicates impairment. Before he can make a traffic stop, you jet into your apartment complex, park your car, and start walking to your apartment. The cop pulls up and chases you to the door. If he saw you driving, or the circumstances were otherwise that it was clear you were driving (no one left in the car, no one else in the area), he can proceed as if he had stopped you on the roadside. You won’t be the first person to try the “Who, me?” defense.

Question: Can people with implants be legally diagnosed as disabled and take up all my famous parking spots?
Answer: I’m not sure why you regard handicapped spaces as your “famous parking spots,” but, otherwise, yes. “Implants” can be hip or knee replacements. Some people gain restored mobility after these implants are installed, but others still experience pain or limited tolerance to walking. If their physician feels they are sufficiently impaired to merit a handicapped parking placard, they can give them the documentation needed to obtain one. The disability of the person holding the placard may not be immediately apparent. My former girlfriend had a degenerative neurological disorder. Sometimes she would be able to walk with no perceptible problem, but when she became fatigued, it would invite what she called a “storm” and her gait would be severely impaired, so much that I occasionally had to go fetch her wheelchair from the car and bring it to her to get back. We got a few dirty looks when we got out of the car at some retail establishments where she didn’t think she would have to walk very far, or when she could use a shopping cart as a support while we went through the store. The moral of the story: don’t judge the person getting out of the car just because they don't have an obvious impairment.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: If police want to get a search warrant for your Google drive, do they have to tell a judge they know they will actually find what they seek on it?
Answer: The Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution reads: The right of the people to be secure in their persons , houses , papers , and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated, and no warrants shall issue, but upon probable cause, supported by Oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized. Emphasis added. In order to obtain a search warrant, the police have to represent to the issuing magistrate what they intend to search (a place or other entity, such as a web account) what evidence they expect to find, and why they think it is evidence of a crime. For a Google Drive, the police would need to state whether they expect to find child pornography, records of criminal transactions, documents describing crimes, or whatever other information they think resides on the drive.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: Do police officers get motorcycles that fit their size?
Answer: In most cases, no. During my tenure, my department had one type of motorcycle in use: Kawasaki K1000s. If you wanted to ride, you had to learn to ride those. It took years for a woman to qualify to ride, as most could not pick up the bike from the ground, a requirement to be motorcycle-qualified. Most officers were of sufficient stature to ride that bike. I know of only one male officer who might have been too short for the bike, and so far as I know, he never applied to go to motorcycle school. Later, the PD deployed some Harley-Davidson bikes. Several officers coveted them because of their “American Iron” reputation, but they were far less reliable than the Kawasakis. Many officers found themselves stranded when their batteries went dead during a traffic stop, and they were unable to start the bike. I don’t know if the H-D bikes would have been more accommodating for shorter officers.

Question: Is it true that the Feds will arrest you with a SWAT team if you get the FAFSA but fail your classes or dropout?
